d6e3c22f29.q: What is the difference between buying marketing assets versus renting marketing results?
d6e3c22f29.a: Every marketing dollar either buys you an asset or rents you a result. When you buy ads, you are renting attention that stops the day you stop paying. When you buy leads, you are renting names that have been sold to multiple advisors. When you build an email list or publish owned content, you own it and it keeps producing clients after you stop paying. Assets keep producing after you stop feeding them money, while expenses produce something only while you pay.

bf4a4e7093.q: Why should financial advisors avoid buying leads for client acquisition?
bf4a4e7093.a: When you buy a lead, you are buying a name that has been sold to multiple financial advisors, and you enter that relationship as a commodity. These prospects are comparison shopping, they don't know you, they don't trust you, and you are the fourth voicemail on their phone that week. You start from a position of weakness instead of building a relationship where you own the prospect.

6d73fba1de.q: How does the effort heuristic principle apply to financial advisor direct mail marketing?
6d73fba1de.a: In 2004, Justin Kruger and colleagues published research showing that people consistently rate high-effort items as better and more valuable than quick efforts. A physical letter addressed to a specific prospect carries perceived effort and value, while LinkedIn messages take 11 seconds and carry no perceived effort. Meanwhile, the physical mailbox is emptier than it has been in decades with less competition, so direct mail combines less competition with more perceived effort—a wonderful combination.

d0a7c50a72.q: Why is holding cash in reserve the most investor-like move in a $10,000 marketing budget?
d0a7c50a72.a: After running your marketing system for 90 days, you learn what works. If direct mail is booking appointments like crazy, you have cash to triple the mailing list. If emails are converting but your website is not, you have money to fix the actual constraint. The advisor who spends everything on day one has zero ability to double down on what works, and doubling down on what works is where all the returns are going to live.
